_doc: Plausibility bands for the occupational distribution of a no-intervention baseline (Complaint 619, DESIGN 4.2). Each trade belongs to one group; each band is the range of the group's share of all working hours that a pre-industrial agrarian economy plausibly shows. The bands are deliberately wide: they say 'not absurd', they are not a fit, and they are not set from any dated year. Shares of the labour force stand in for shares of hours (hours per worker differ by trade; that difference is smaller than the width of the bands). Every figure below is RECALLED from the named literature, not looked up in this session; check against the source before narrowing a band. 'unattributed' holds the unskilled labourer pool whose hours recipes do not assign to an occupation; its band caps how much of the economy may stay unclassified.

sources.scheidel_friesen_2009: Scheidel and Friesen, 'The Size of the Economy and the Distribution of Income in the Roman Empire', Journal of Roman Studies 99 (2009). Recalled: the large majority of the empire's people lived and worked on the land; the urban share was roughly one tenth to one sixth.
sources.allen_2000: Allen, 'Economic structure and agricultural productivity in Europe, 1300-1800', European Review of Economic History 4 (2000). Recalled: agriculture takes well over half of the labour force in pre-industrial European economies, four fifths or more in the poorest.
sources.bairoch_1988: Bairoch, Cities and Economic Development (1988). Recalled: pre-industrial economies keep roughly two thirds to nine tenths of the labour force in agriculture.
sources.broadberry_2015: Broadberry, Campbell, Klein, Overton, van Leeuwen, British Economic Growth 1270-1870 (2015). Recalled: textiles are the largest single industrial employer, from a low single-digit share of all workers up to the mid-teens; building a few percent.
sources.wilson_2002: Wilson, 'Machines, Power and the Ancient Economy', Journal of Roman Studies 92 (2002), and Wilson and Flohr (eds), The Economy of Roman Italy (2016). Recalled, qualitative only: cloth, building and food processing were the main non-farm trades.

ordering._doc: Textiles or building is expected to be the largest non-farm group among those classified (Complaint 619).
